bull_case: VAS and money movement provide high-return adjacent reinvestment opportunities while buybacks compound per-share cash flow.
bear_case: If incentives rise faster than gross revenue and new rails reduce pricing, incremental returns can compress.
thesis: Visa has high-quality FCF/share compounding and a long reinvestment runway, though conventional capex/R&D absorption metrics understate reinvestment because much network investment runs through operating expense and client incentives.

evidence.claim: FY2025 owner-style FCF proxy was $20.68B, about $10.52 per diluted Class A share.

counterevidence: Regulatory and interchange litigation can pressure network economics and pricing over time.
The current valuation already embeds a high-quality compounder profile.
unknowns: Long-run regulation of interchange and routing
Sustainable growth rate of Visa Direct and value-added services
falsifiers: If processed transactions and payments volume decelerate materially while client incentives rise faster than gross revenue, the moat/FCF thesis weakens.

hard_veto_flags.rationale: Strong cash conversion, low incremental capital needs and expanding VAS contradict a structural collapse in incremental ROIC.
Visa is a large net repurchaser; dilution is not persistent/excessive.

next_checks: Payments volume, cross-border volume, processed transactions, value-added services, client incentives, owner FCF/share, buyback price

subscores.rationale: Asset-light network economics convert growth into large cash flow with low incremental physical capital needs.
Reported capex understates economic reinvestment because Visa reinvests through technology, client incentives, tokenization, acquisitions and VAS; multiple long-run growth paths remain.
Owner-style FCF is very high and buybacks reduce the share denominator while SBC is modest relative to OCF.

uncertainties.rationale: Regulation, incentives and valuation are the main uncertainty.
Regulation, incentives and valuation are the main uncertainty.
